title: Drones and Death: Families Reel from the UAE’s “Catastrophic” Strikes in War on ISIS
author: Mohamed Gabobe

MOGADISHU, Somalia--Drones had been hovering over Togga-Xarago--a mountainous
settlement in northeastern Somalia all day. The Reer Yusuf Mohamud Salah
family was used to the noise; it was a regular occurrence in the Al-Miskaad
mountains, where the Puntland security forces are waging an on-going war
against ISIS militants, supported by the UAE and now the U.S.

On the evening of January 26, 2025, as her family gathered for dinner in their
traditional Somali style hut known as an _Caqil Soomaali_ , 38-year-old Khadra
Abdi Ismael went to a neighbor's home to retrieve an item for her relatives.
Moments later, Khadra heard the large engine roars of an aircraft hovering
above.

A large explosion followed. Thick smoke billowed through the sky as screams
could be heard from the ruins of the hut, Khadra told Drop Site.

"The Caqil Soomaali was engulfed in flames, and smoke was everywhere," Khadra
said.

"Once the smoke cleared, the true horrors emerged: I saw shrapnel from the
missile and body parts strewn everywhere," she said. "Even the livestock were
ripped to pieces."

Four of her family members were killed and five were wounded. Khadra's older
sister, Ladan Abdi Ismael, and her 13-year-old son Abdisamad Yusuf Mohamud
were both killed alongside seven-year-old Mohamed Abdiqani Mohamed and
17-year-old Hawa Ahmed Salah, who was four months pregnant. Salah was holding
her 8-month-old child on her lap--who miraculously survived the drone strike.

"The child survived but she didn't," Khadra tells Drop Site.

Four separate security officials from the semi-autonomous Puntland region
confirmed to Drop Site that the strike on January 26, 2025 targeting the Reer
Yusuf Mohamud Salah family in the vicinity of Togga-Xarago was carried out by
the United Arab Emirates. They were granted anonymity to speak about sensitive
issues.

Drop Site reached out to the UAE embassy in Mogadishu and the UAE Ministry for
Foreign Affairs for comment on the airstrike, as well as their operations from
the military base in Bosasso. The Emirati diplomatic mission in Mogadishu or
UAE foreign affairs did not respond to our queries.

There is currently no official, comprehensive data available on the exact
number of civilian casualties in the war on ISIS. The airstrikes and clashes
take place in remote, mountainous areas inhabited by small, isolated Bedouin
communities. These areas are difficult for journalists, human rights
organizations, and media outlets to access, making it extremely challenging to
establish the full human cost of the conflict.

Puntland security officials add that the drones used in the strike set off
from a UAE military base on the grounds of the airport in Bosasso. Those
drones, the security officials say, are used for the sole purpose of counter
terrorism operations in the Puntland region, targeting fighters of the Islamic
State active in the Al-Miskaad mountains, with the UAE carrying out numerous
strikes targeting militants during the first quarter of 2025, which picked
back up during the last quarter of 2025.

A second Puntland security official interviewed by Drop Site stated that the
UAE military base at Bosasso was more expansive than the current U.S. presence
at the airport, which is limited to an intelligence command center where
AFRICOM and CIA personnel are stationed, aligning with [recent
findings](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/new-us-base-somalia-airstrikes-isis-
al-shabaab-cia) by Drop Site.

Just weeks before the January 26 strike, the Reer Yusuf Mohamud Salah family
had been living in the settlement of Dhadaar in the Al-Miskaad mountains,
which they have called home for generations.

In early December, government forces had informed the Bedouin family and
others in Dhadaar that this was an area where ISIS was present, and ordered
them to leave. Ahmed Abdi Ismael, the brother of Khadra similarly told Drop
Site that his family was ordered by government forces to leave the area and
relocate to a designated "safe zone" to be spared from the fighting against
ISIS.

"My family was among many people that fled after being ordered to move by the
government," Ahmed said. "They were told to move and that this new area would
be safe from the fighting, but they were bombed anyway."

The family is still devastated by the effects of the strike. Habibo Yusuf
Mohamud, who was pregnant at the time, "lost movement in her arm and still has
shrapnel lodged in her neck," Khadra told Drop Site. "Every time she tries to
turn her neck, she feels excruciating pain."

The Reer Yusuf Mohamud Salah family also lost six camels and 400 goats,
destroying the family's livelihood by eliminating their only source of income.

Following the UAE drone strike, the wounded survivors were moved on their
neighbors' camels, eventually reaching the government-controlled town of
Balidhidin. In 2021, ISIS militants assassinated the mayor of Balidhidin, and
fighters loyal to the group are still believed to be active in the area. From
there, those with more serious injuries were transported to the port city of
Bosasso for better medical treatment.

In January 2025 during the start of the war against ISIS in the Al-Miskaad
mountains in the Puntland region, the UAE was not only carrying out drone
strikes but air dropping supplies to Puntland ground forces with large cargo
planes in areas of the Al-Miskaad mountains, where reliable road access was
non existent.

Since November 2025, the UAE has not carried out a drone strike in the
Puntland region of Somalia and since the start of this year, their anti terror
operations have lessened, despite ISIS remaining an active threat in the Al-
Miskaad mountains of Somalia. According to Puntland security officials, the
U.S. has taken the lead and is currently spearheading the war against ISIS in
the Puntland region.

As UAE drone strikes have halted in 2026, the Emirates are still remain
actively involved in security operations in Puntland in support of local
forces, in particular the Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF), tasked with
combating armed non-state Islamist actors and anti-piracy operations.

The United Arab Emirates supports the PMPF with training, pays their salaries,
and collaborates with them in intelligence gathering. The extensive Emirati
support has transformed the PMPF into the most powerful state security
apparatus in Puntland.

The current director general of the PMPF is a close family member of
Puntland's ruling leader Said Deni; as of October 9, the Puntland regional
president is currently in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, Puntland
security officials privy to his itinerary told Drop Site.

The Puntland security officials that spoke with Drop Site declined to go into
further details about the purpose of the Puntland's president's trip to the
UAE, with one Puntland security official simply saying, "He traveled alone."

"Our family hasn't returned to the area [Togga-Xarago] because there isn't
anything to return to because we lost all our livestock in the strike," Khadra
said. "Even here in Balidhidan, we still see planes flying over, and it
reminds us of what happened to our family that night."

Four Puntland security officials with intricate knowledge on UAE military
operations in Puntland have told Drop Site that UAE drone strikes have been
"catastrophic" and at times "reckless."

"When the US carries out a strike, their is a lot of surveillance that takes
place beforehand. Oftentimes, the US surveillance drones will carry out
reconnaissance on a target in the mountains for a lengthy period of time, then
carry out a lethal strike but the Emirates fire on anything that moves," a
Puntland security official tells Drop Site.

"With the Emirates, there is no level of accountability. If they see a group
of people burning wood somewhere in the [Al-Miskaad] mountains, they won't
even care to verify if these individuals are nomads or Daesh [ISIS]," a second
Puntland security official said.

"It's like target practice for them," he said.
